name: New Caledonia
summary_text: New Caledonia is a French collectivity in which France retains responsibility for penal law, civil-status documents and the justice system, while the territory legislates locally on many domestic matters. The protections a trans visitor would rely on are therefore French national provisions that apply here as French law, and no source in this inventory records a local ordinance narrowing them. Nothing in the inventory criminalises trans people or same-sex relations.  Same-sex marriage has been available in New Caledonia since France's 2013 marriage-equality statute, which applies here as French law. CNN reported on 29 May 2013 on the first same-sex wedding solemnised in France under that law. PinkNews reported on 26 August 2012 that the French government would introduce its same-sex marriage and adoption bill into Parliament in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge.  Sexual identity became a ground of discrimination in the French Penal Code through the sexual-harassment legislation of 2012, which enabled prosecution of discrimination and of transphobia as discrimination; the provision was amended in 2016 to read gender identity. As French law, the provision reaches New Caledonia.  Placement of detainees follows the legal gender marker rather than anatomy: Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code assigns incarcerated trans people according to their recorded sex, which in practice places trans women in all-male facilities where they face threats of assault by other detainees (BuzzFeed News, 12 January 2018). The French prison framework governs the collectivity's establishments in the same way.  France's detention-places watchdog, the CGLPL, reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of the rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty. Its findings rest on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on inspections at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. Because French law applies here, the opinion extends to establishments in New Caledonia.

sources.title: French Penal Code of 1791 and Penal Code of 1810
sources.documents: Baseline decriminalisation of same-sex sexual activity in private in France; article states policy was retained in 1810 Code and followed in nations and French colonies that adopted the Code - foundation for legality in New Caledonia as French territory.
sources.detail: No URL visible in text. Citation detail visible: 'Penal Code of 1791 made no mention of same-sex relations in private' and 'retained in the Penal Code of 1810'.

sources.title: Law of 4 August 1982 equalising age of consent - repeal of article 331 (ex-article 334)
sources.documents: Equalised age of consent at 15 for same- and opposite-sex relations by repealing Vichy-era discriminatory provision that had raised it to 21 then 18 for homosexual relations.
sources.detail: No URL visible. Citation detail visible: 'article 334 (moved to article 331 on 8 February 1945)' 'remained valid until 4 August 1982, when it was repealed under President François Mitterrand to equalise the age of consent at 15'.

sources.title: Same-sex marriage law of 2013 - National Assembly / Senate votes and Constitutional Council ruling of 17 May 2013
sources.documents: Legalises same-sex marriage and joint adoption; article expressly states 'Same-sex marriage is legal in all of France's overseas departments and territories' including New Caledonia.
sources.detail: No URL visible. Citation detail visible: 'National Assembly approved the bill as a whole in a 329-229 vote' 'Senate approved the bill' 'On 17 May 2013, the Council ruled that the law is constitutional' 'signed 18 May 2013' 'published the next day in the Journal Officiel' 'first official same-sex ceremony took place on 29 May in Montpellier'.

sources.title: Law of 18 November 2016 on legal gender change - published in Journal Officiel 19 November 2016, effective 1 January 2017
sources.documents: Allows transgender people to legally change gender without sex reassignment surgery, sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or medical diagnosis; requires court application; first-name change via registry office. Core trans legal-status source applicable in New Caledonia.
sources.detail: No URL visible. Citation detail visible: 'On 6 November 2015, bill approved by Senate' '24 May 2016 National Assembly approved' '12 July 2016 National Assembly approved modified version' '12 October plenary' '17 November Constitutional Council ruled bill constitutional' 'signed 18 November 2016, published in Journal Officiel the next day, took effect 1 January 2017'.

sources.title: European Court of Human Rights - B. vs France (1992)
sources.documents: Ended decades-long French legislative ban on legal gender change even after medical/surgical transition; established ECHR-based right to gender-marker change in France.
sources.detail: No URL visible. Citation detail visible: 'French legislature then banned legal gender change for people for many decades, even if they had undergone medical and surgical transition, until a 1992 case, B. vs France at the European Court of Human Rights changed this'.

sources.title: Article 225-1 French Penal Code as amended 18 November 2016 + Labour Code Chapter 2 (Code du travail)

sources.title: Law of 31 December 2004 / 30 December 2004 creating Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité + amendment to Law on Freedom of the Press of 29 July 1881
sources.documents: Hate-crime / hate-speech enforcement machinery: criminalises homophobic, sexist, racist comments (45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months imprisonment cited), creates High Authority against Discrimination, increases penalties when assault/murder motivated by sexual orientation; 2017 extension making transphobia aggravating factor for imprisonable crimes.
sources.detail: No URL visible. Citation detail visible: 'On 31 December 2004, National Assembly approved amendment' 'law of December 2004 created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité' 'Title 3 and articles 20 and 21 amended Law on Freedom of Press of 29 July 1881' 'In 2017, transphobia became a cause of aggravation for all crimes that can be punished by prison'.

sources.title: ILGA-Europe 2022 report on gender affirming healthcare in France
sources.documents: Documents significant issues with provision of gender affirming healthcare in France: lack of self-determination, extended waiting times, inequitable access by location; recommends informed-consent/self-determination system. Directly relevant to trans visitor healthcare expectations.
sources.detail: No URL visible. Citation detail visible: 'A report published in 2022 by ILGA-Europe found significant issues with the provision of gender affirming healthcare in France, including lack of self-determination, extended waiting times, and inequitable access depending on location'.
